t: Introduction: topic, aim and lecture plan
n: In this lecture we consider the ethical foundations of experiments on humans and animals. Experiments on humans and animals are necessary for medicine, but they raise grave ethical questions. The aim is to master the rules of consent, patients' rights and humane treatment of animals. The lecture has five parts: Nuremberg and consent, pharmaceutical bioethics, evidence-based medicine, animal experiments and the 3R principle.

t: International medical-ethical codes and organisations
n: The WHO and the World Medical Association, that is, the WMA, recognise differing ethical views and regulate them through international codes and agreements. The Lisbon Declaration on the Rights of the Patient and the European Declaration are very important for informed consent. Attention, there is a risk of error: the Lisbon Declaration was adopted by the WMA in 1981, and the European Declaration by the WHO in 1994. Do not confuse the organisation and the year. Predictive medicine can identify a predisposition to disease. The question arises: how should consent to treatment be obtained when there is no pain?

t: The Nuremberg trial: historical background
n: Now we consider the historical background of the Nuremberg trial. In 1947 in Germany, US Military Tribunal I tried medical personnel. The concept of informed consent began to take shape precisely at this time. The trial of 23 leading German physician-scientists ended on 20 August 1947. The International Military Tribunal classified these acts as a crime against humanity. The Hippocratic Oath did not stop the German physicians. The trial showed how fragile the boundary between good and evil is.

t: Types of experiments exposed at the Nuremberg trial
n: Several types of experiments were exposed at the Nuremberg trial. The American prosecutor Telford Taylor, in his opening statement, presented the court with a number of facts about the experiments. They are shown in the table: altitude and cold experiments at Dachau; malaria and mustard gas at Dachau and Sachsenhausen; wounds and transplantation at Ravensbrück; drinking of seawater, again at Dachau. The experiments were conducted on prisoners of war and prisoners, and their consent was not sought. What matters is not scientific value but the absence of consent. The tribunal called this a crime against humanity.

t: The Nuremberg trial in figures
n: Let us look at the Nuremberg trial in figures. On 20 August 1947 the court concluded the case against the defendants, 23 leading German medical scientists. In one concentration camp, 1200 healthy people were infected with malaria, and 30 of them died directly of malaria. The Code was adopted in the form of a court decision, but it had moral, not legal, force. It contains ten principles, that is, 10. The first principle: the voluntary consent of the subject of the experiment is essential. Consent must be given without violence, deceit or pressure.

t: The Nuremberg Code: structure and significance
n: Let us dwell on the structure and significance of the Nuremberg Code. A section entitled “Permissible Medical Experiments” was included in the verdict of the tribunal. It then became an independent document under the name “Nuremberg Code”. The Code became the first international document regulating the conduct of medical experiments on humans, and consists of 10 principles. It was adopted in the form of a court verdict, but its moral force is greater than its legal force. For the first time the interests of the individual human being were placed above the interests of science and society. The Code serves as a model to this day.

t: First principle: conditions of voluntary consent
n: The first principle of the Code: the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential. Consent must be given without violence, deceit, fraud or hidden forms of pressure. Voluntary consent consists of five conditions: capacity, that is, the ability to give consent; free choice, that is, without coercion or deceit; understanding, that is, knowledge of the details of the experiment; knowledge, that is, sufficient knowledge and comprehension; and decision, that is, a considered decision. Attention: today what is required is not voluntary but informed consent. This is a stricter norm.

t: Voluntary consent and informed consent
n: The concept of “voluntary consent” was used for the first time in paragraph 1 of the Nuremberg Code. Voluntary consent requires free choice without violence, deceit or pressure, and an understanding of the details of the experiment. Informed consent, by contrast, is a free decision based on information, and it is used in present-day legal and ethical guidelines. In it, the aim, risk and alternatives are explained in understandable language. Attention: these two terms are not the same. In present-day documents, informed consent is regarded as the stricter norm.

t: Evolution of informed consent: US court practice
n: Let us see how the concept of informed consent developed. This concept began to be applied in the USA in court cases on compensation for harm from improper treatment. The chronology is as follows: in 1947 the Nuremberg Code introduced voluntary consent. In the 1950s and 60s the physician was obliged to inform the patient about medical risk and alternative forms of treatment; in this period the information was professional in character. In the 1970s, patient-oriented, understandable information was required. Today, in a US court, consent is a legal criterion of how far the physician cared for the patient.

t: Paternalism and the legal protection of the patient
n: Let us compare paternalism and the legal protection of the patient. Paternalism is a model of fatherly care: the physician, having studied the patient's condition, chose the method of treatment himself, and consent also depended on this. Informed consent, by contrast, protects the patient legally: on the basis of information the patient gives consent. The patient's rights include giving consent and refusing it, and receiving information about his health; the institution ensures this. Informed consent removes the natural inequality between patient and physician, since the patient is dependent on the physician.

t: Patient rights in Uzbekistan
n: Patient rights in Uzbekistan are laid down by law. There is a natural inequality between patient and physician; its compensation is to provide the patient with full legal protection. Under the law “On the Protection of Citizens' Health”, the patient has the right to respect, to choice of physician and to confidentiality. The diagram shows these rights: respect; choice; conditions meeting sanitary requirements; confidentiality of the consultation and diagnosis; voluntary consent or refusal; compensation for harm; and the right to call a lawyer. If rights are violated, the patient or his legal representative may apply to the head of the institution or to a court.

t: Case analysis 1: consent and coercion
n: Case analysis: consent and coercion. In the Dachau camp, prisoners were tested under conditions corresponding to an altitude of 12 km. The aim was to help German pilots. Question: which principle of the Nuremberg Code was violated? The first principle: the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential. In the Code, for the first time in history, the interests of the individual were placed above the interests of science and society, so the argument of “benefit to society” does not hold. Attention: voluntary consent is not the same as informed consent. In present-day guidelines the latter is the stricter norm.

t: Quick question 1: Nuremberg and consent
n: The first block of quick questions: Nuremberg and consent. First question: when, and by which tribunal, was the Nuremberg Code prepared? Answer: in 1947, by US Military Tribunal I. Second question: how many principles does the Code contain, and what is the first about? Answer: ten; voluntary consent. Third question: what does voluntary consent require of the individual? Answer: legal capacity, free choice without coercion, and understanding of the details. Fourth question: what is the difference between voluntary and informed consent? Answer: informed consent is the stricter norm.

t: The thalidomide tragedy and pharmaceutical bioethics
n: Now we turn to the thalidomide tragedy and pharmaceutical bioethics. Pregnant women were given a sleeping drug, and children were born without arms and legs. After that the aim of science changed: alongside developing a new drug, preventing harm also became an aim. The interval between development and clinical use was several weeks in the early 1960s, and by the early 1980s had stretched to 10 years. The cost rose more than 20-fold. Pharmaceutical bioethics studies the ethical problems from drug development to the consumer.

t: The Declaration of Helsinki: history of its formation
n: Let us see how the Declaration of Helsinki took shape. Because of thalidomide, about 20 thousand children were born without limbs; in Japan the drug caused the disease “SMON”. This alarmed the World Medical Association, which adopted the declaration in Helsinki in 1964. It was then supplemented: Tokyo 1975, Venice 1984, Hong Kong 1989, Somerset West 1996, Edinburgh 2000. The table shows the years of revision in sequence.

t: Ethics committees and Good Clinical Practice (GCP)
n: On ethics committees and Good Clinical Practice. According to the Helsinki–Tokyo recommendations, an independent commission or committee must oversee research protocols. Then the rules of GCP, that is, Good Clinical Practice, were developed. The World Health Organization recommends that the committee be independent of political, departmental and financial influence. The path of ethical review is as follows: the research protocol is ready; the independent committee reviews it; an ethical review opinion is issued; if there is an opinion, the trial begins; and the committee continues to oversee it.

t: The European Convention, the Belmont Report, committees of Uzbekistan
n: On the European Convention and the committees of Uzbekistan. In 1993 the General Assembly of the Council of Europe adopted the convention on the protection of human rights and dignity in biology and medicine. In Uzbekistan a Bioethics Committee operates under the Ministry of Health, headed by Academician M.S. Abdullakhodjaeva; there is also a National Committee under the Ibn Sina Foundation. The committee relies on the Constitution, the 1996 healthcare law, the 1997 law on medicines, the Declaration of Helsinki and GCP.

t: Case analysis 2: a drug trial and ethical review
n: Case analysis: a drug trial and ethical review. A new drug is ready for clinical trial, but there is no opinion of moral, that is, ethical, review. According to the source, today no country in the West allows experiments on humans without an opinion of moral review. The committee in Uzbekistan relies on the Constitution, the laws on healthcare and on medicines, the Declaration of Helsinki, the Belmont Report, GCP and WHO recommendations. Question: why is such a trial impossible? Must the ethics committee be independent of political, departmental and financial influence?

t: Evidence-based medicine: Cochrane and randomisation
n: Evidence-based medicine is linked with Cochrane and randomisation. In 1972 Cochrane stressed that society was unaware of the real effectiveness of drugs. Randomisation is the random allocation of patients to a study group and a control group. In 1992 the first Cochrane Centre was opened in Oxford; at the 1993 colloquium 73 representatives from 9 countries took part. The process of a systematic review is as follows: systematic collection of data, analysis, preparation of a scientific review, updating with new data, and publication in the Cochrane database.

t: Main reasons for the spread of evidence-based medicine
n: Scientifically proven, that is, evidence-based, medicine uses only methods whose effectiveness has been proven. The term “evidence-based medicine” was introduced by specialists at McMaster University in Canada. There are four reasons for its spread: uncertain effectiveness, since even old drugs were not rigorously tested; quality improvement, that is, well-founded, reliable, economical decisions; information technology, that is, the computer; and new thinking, that is, a view based on critical analysis. Attention: a new or expensive drug does not mean an effective drug. Effectiveness is confirmed only by evidence.

t: The Cochrane Library: four databases
n: On the Cochrane Library. In October 1992 the first Cochrane Centre was opened in Oxford; at the first colloquium in 1993, 73 representatives from 9 countries took part. The Cochrane Library is an electronic database on evidence-based medicine, consisting of four separate databases: systematic reviews, the effectiveness base, the trials register and the methodology base. The database of systematic reviews summarises the results of randomised controlled trials. Access to tables of contents and abstracts is free; full texts require a subscription.

t: Economic and ethical aspects of evidence-based medicine
n: Let us consider the economic and ethical aspect of evidence-based medicine. The novelty or high price of a drug does not guarantee its effectiveness. According to various data, only 30 to 50 per cent of medical interventions have undergone large-scale clinical trials. The physician must be able to distinguish scientifically grounded information from descriptive or covert advertising. Attention: both a cheap but ineffective drug, and prescribing an expensive drug when a cheap one with a similar result is available, increase costs.

t: Ethics and law: difference and interrelation
n: Let us determine the difference between ethics and law. Attention: the concept of “ethics” is broader than “law”; they are not the same thing. Law demands compliance with rules, is fixed by statute and is a legal obligation; its scope is narrower. Ethics demands honesty and disinterestedness, cannot be regulated by law, and before taking legal form serves as a guarantee of safety; its scope is broader. In biomedical research, questions of ethics and law are interrelated, which is why they are considered together. Some aspects of the physician–patient relationship are not yet regulated by law.

t: Case analysis 3: advertising, price and effectiveness
n: Case analysis: advertising, price and effectiveness. A patient asks for an expensive drug found on the internet to be prescribed, while the physician has found neither the time nor the means to find such information. According to the source, it is hard to imagine a more dangerous situation. In informed consent the physician offers information and helps the patient to assess it critically. Question: what does evidence-based medicine offer here? The physician must independently seek new information, assess it critically and introduce it into practice.

t: Quick question 2: pharmaceutical bioethics and Cochrane
n: The second block of quick questions. First question: when and where was the Declaration of Helsinki adopted? Answer: in June 1964, in Helsinki, at the 18th General Assembly of the World Medical Association. Second question: what is randomisation? Answer: the random allocation of patients to a study group and a control group. Third question: what is GCP? Answer: Good Clinical Practice, rules developed after the declaration. Fourth question: where was the first Cochrane Centre opened? Answer: in Oxford, in October 1992. Attention: Cochrane's idea, 1972, is not the same as the opening of the centre, 1992.

t: Three stages in the history of animal experiments
n: The history of animal experiments consists of three stages. Ibn Sina considered experiment on animals the most reliable way to study the action of drugs. Ibn Zuhr tested new drugs on animals before using them on people. The first stage falls in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries: Vesalius performed vivisection without anaesthesia, since analgesics were discovered only at the beginning of the nineteenth century. In the second stage public discontent arose, and in 1878 a law was passed. The third stage begins in the 1920s and is linked with the use of animals in education and with international recommendations.

t: Vivisection and public attitudes
n: On vivisection and public attitudes. Analgesics were discovered at the beginning of the nineteenth century, so vivisection was extremely cruel. Because torture was commonplace, the public in practice did not voice an opinion on the cruelty of vivisection. Darwin's teaching showed the kinship of humans with animals; in 1878 a law protecting animals was passed in Great Britain. Claude Bernard placed dogs, rabbits and pigeons in special ovens to study the effect of high temperature; the animals perished at 90–100 °C.

t: The twentieth century: documents and international recommendations
n: In the twentieth century, documents and international recommendations appeared. Physicians also joined the movement to restrict animal experiments. The timeline is as follows: in the 1920s dissection of animals appeared in the curriculum, and vivisection entered teaching. According to the 1981 code of teaching practice, a student may perform on vertebrate animals only experiments that are painless and safe for human health. In 1984 the advisory committee of the Council of Europe approved international recommendations. In 1986 the Strasbourg Convention established the protection of vertebrate animals. Despite the law and public opinion, cruel experiments are still carried out today.

t: Why animal experiments are considered necessary
n: Why are animal experiments considered necessary? It is held that genetics, biochemistry, physiology, pharmacology, toxicology and hygiene could not be investigated without animal experiments. The discoveries of scientists such as Pasteur, Bernard, Magendie, Sechenov and Pavlov rested on animal experiments. The effects of poison, wounds, ionising radiation and infectious agents are not tested on humans, so the model is created in an animal. Ibn Sina also considered experiment on animals the most reliable way to study the action of drugs.

t: Arguments against animal experiments
n: Now we consider the arguments against animal experiments. In the view of Fox, USA, vivisection hinders the shift to disease prevention, and models reflect the clinical picture poorly. In the view of Inglis, mortality from infectious disease fell thanks to improved sanitation and living conditions; in Britain it is said to have fallen by as much as 92 per cent. In the clofibrate trial, 1964 to 1972, World Health Organization, 10 thousand men, total mortality turned out 37 per cent higher than among those who did not receive the drug. Coleman, Great Britain, writes that he cannot recall a single important achievement resulting from animal experiments. This is the position of the critics.

t: Species differences: why drug action changes
n: Species differences change the action of drugs. Thalidomide was not teratogenic in animal experiments; the risk appeared only in humans and in rarely used animals. Examples in the table: thalidomide has a teratogenic effect on the human foetus, and is harmless to rodents. Morphine calms a human but excites a cat. Aspirin does not cause birth defects in humans but causes defects in mice and rats. Insulin is harmless to humans and harmful to laboratory animals. The metabolism of phenylbutazone lasts 72 hours in humans, and only 6 hours in the dog and the rat. When 23 compounds were compared, human and rat metabolism proceeded in the same way in only four.

t: Case analysis 4: isoprenaline and thalidomide
n: Case analysis: isoprenaline and thalidomide. In the 1960s in Great Britain, 3.5 thousand asthma patients who used isoprenaline aerosol inhalers died. In animals even large doses only slightly increased the heart rate; the cat tolerated a dose 175 times larger than a human. In a human even a small dose may cause arrhythmia. The same is true of thalidomide: it was found harmless in animal experiments, and about ten thousand children were born with defects. Question: what risks arise from transferring an animal result to humans, that is, extrapolation? How does cell culture, the 3R principle, reduce this?

t: The 3R principle: Replacement, Reduction, Refinement
n: The 3R principle is a bioethical concept aimed at the replacement, reduction and refinement of the use of animals. In 1926 a society was founded at the University of London; since 1938 it has operated under the name UFAW, that is, the Universities Federation for Animal Welfare. Replacement: replacing the animal with an alternative method, for example cell culture or a chick embryo. Reduction: a justified reduction in the number of animals, and avoidance of repeated experiments. Refinement: reducing stress and pain, with analgesics.

t: Alternative methods and research centres
n: Alternative methods and research centres exist. ECVAM, that is, the European Centre for the Validation of Alternative Methods, in the city of Ispra, the Nottingham Foundation and the “Alternative Centre” in Berlin are at work. Methods in the table: cell culture gives in-depth analysis, is cheap, uses human cells, and is applied in virology, oncology and vaccinology. A single-celled organism is convenient and cheap. The chick embryo is cheap, simple and reliable, and is used to determine the action of an agent. Computer models are also counted as an alternative. An alternative method is not always possible: many experiments must be conducted not on a simple system but on a whole organism. GLP, that is, good laboratory practice, sometimes requires a new product to be tested on animals.

t: General ethical requirements when working with animals
n: There are general ethical requirements when working with animals. Article 25 of the Council of Europe convention: experiments are not performed on animals if a scientifically satisfactory method without animals exists. Directive 86/609/EEC also rests on this. An experiment is permissible only for a necessary purpose and where there is reason to expect benefit. Unnecessary repetition is not permitted; the number of animals and the methodology are approved in advance. Animals are obtained from certified breeding establishments, and stray animals are not permitted. The experiment is performed by a qualified researcher; the laboratory meets GLP requirements.

t: Orders of biomodels and the vivarium
n: On the orders of biomodels and the vivarium. A first-order model is laboratory animals; second-order, bacteria and cell cultures; third-order, mathematical models. The suitability of a biomodel is assessed by four criteria: structure, that is, morphological similarity; function, that is, metabolic, neurohumoral, exocrine; response, that is, similarity of reaction to an external influence; and constants, that is, correspondence of quantitative indices to the original. After the monkey, the mini-pig is the model closest to humans: blood pressure, skin and atherosclerotic plaques are similar. The beagle is a widely used model. Animals are kept in a vivarium, that is, a department for care and breeding.

t: Choosing laboratory animals and forming groups
n: Let us consider choosing laboratory animals and forming groups. The choice of animal species depends on the task of the study. Surgical experiments are more often performed on large animals, that is, dogs, calves, monkeys and pigs. For studying the action of pharmacological drugs, small laboratory animals are convenient: mice, rats and guinea pigs. Experimental groups are formed to be equivalent in species, sex, age and weight of the animals. All groups are introduced into the experiment at the same time and kept under identical conditions.

t: Immobilisation and anaesthesia: reducing pain
n: Immobilisation and anaesthesia are needed to reduce pain. Proper handling calms the animal, reduces fear and pain, and also protects the staff. The stages of anaesthesia: first premedication, that is, sedation; then fixation, that is, immobilisation; then administration of the anaesthetic; and monitoring of respiration and reflexes. Methods of anaesthesia: inhalational, enteral, that is, rectal and oral, parenteral, spinal and combined. Premedication is needed before anaesthesia; cats and rabbits are highly sensitive to chloroform.

t: History of anaesthesia: from ether to chloroform
n: Let us dwell on the history of anaesthesia. Anaesthesia is an artificially induced reversible inhibition of the central nervous system, in which the sensation of pain disappears. In animal experiments, preventing pain during surgery or euthanasia is an important aspect. Diethyl ether was discovered in the thirteenth century by Raymond Lull; its analgesic property was described in 1540 by Paracelsus. In 1845 in Boston, Wells demonstrated tooth extraction under “laughing gas”, but the demonstration failed because the dose was wrongly calculated. In 1846 Morton demonstrated ether anaesthesia. In 1847 ether was used in Russia by Inozemtsev and Pirogov, and chloroform was used in childbirth by Simpson.

t: Case analysis 5: choice of anaesthetic and refinement
n: Case analysis: choice of anaesthetic and refinement. An operation is planned on a rabbit and a cat; the usual mixed morphine–ether–chloroform anaesthesia is chosen. The rabbit and the cat are highly sensitive to chloroform and die quickly from it; in the cat, morphine does not inhibit but, on the contrary, excites and causes convulsions. Analysis: this is refinement, that is, reducing distress and pain. The experimenter gives premedication, atropine, uses a little ether instead of chloroform, and watches the respiration. Question: which R is being carried out, and what should the experimenter do? Attention: a dose safe for one species is not suitable for another.

t: Conclusion: ethical limits of experiments on humans and animals
n: Let us conclude. Voluntary consent is the first principle of the Nuremberg Code. Today informed consent is required, which is a stricter norm. Research is reviewed by independent ethics committees; this is a requirement of the Declaration of Helsinki and GCP. Effectiveness is verified by evidence-based medicine. In animals the 3R is applied: replacement, reduction, refinement. If an alternative method exists, the animal is not used; the laboratory must meet GLP requirements.
